title: Βουλὴ περὶ τῶν νεῶν
titleEn: The Counsel About the Ships — Iliad 14.1–108
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Nestor, drinking with the wounded Machaon, hears the shouting by the ships. He tells Machaon to stay and have his wounds washed while he goes to look, takes his son Thrasymedes’ shield and a spear, and from outside the hut sees the Achaean wall fallen and the army in confusion. Torn between joining the fighters and going to Agamemnon, he chooses Agamemnon, and on the way meets the wounded kings Diomedes, Odysseus and Agamemnon coming up from the ships; the poet pauses to say how the ships were drawn up on the beach. Agamemnon fears that Hector’s threat to burn the ships is coming true, and Nestor answers that the wall is down and nothing can now be changed. Agamemnon then proposes launching the nearest ships and escaping by night, and Odysseus rebukes him bitterly. Agamemnon takes the rebuke and asks for a better plan.

sentences.t:
Νέστορα δ’ οὐκ ἔλαθεν ἰαχὴ πίνοντά περ ἔμπης,
ἀλλ’ Ἀσκληπιάδην ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.tr:
Nestora d’ ouk elathen iachē pinonta per empēs,
all’ Asklēpiadēn epea pteroenta prosēuda·
sentences.l:
And Nestor the cry did not escape, drinking though he was, all the same,
but to Asclepius’-son winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: For all his drinking, the cry did not escape Nestor, but he spoke winged words to the son of Asclepius:
sentences.n: Νέστορα is the object of ἔλαθεν: λανθάνω ‘escape the notice of’ takes the accusative of the person who fails to notice, and ἰαχή ‘cry’ is the subject. πίνοντά περ is a participle with concessive περ, ‘drinking though he was’, and ἔμπης ‘all the same’ closes the thought; ἀλλ’ turns to what he did instead. Ἀσκληπιάδην is a patronymic, ‘son of Asclepius’, and names Machaon, whom Nestor addresses in the next line. ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα is the stock phrase that introduces a speech.

sentences.t: φράζεο δῖε Μαχᾶον ὅπως ἔσται τάδε ἔργα·
sentences.tr: phrazeo die Machaon hopōs estai tade erga·
sentences.l: “Consider, heavenly Machaon, how these deeds shall be;
sentences.i: “Consider, heavenly Machaon, how these things are to turn out;
sentences.n: φράζεο is the imperative of φράζομαι ‘consider, take heed’ in an uncontracted form (Attic φράζου), and ὅπως ἔσται, with the future, asks how things will turn out. Μαχᾶον is the vocative of Μαχάων, with δῖε ‘heavenly’, the stock adjective. τάδε ἔργα ‘these deeds’ are the fighting whose noise has just reached Nestor. The same words come back in his mouth at 61, in a line that also stands at 4.14.

sentences.t: μείζων δὴ παρὰ νηυσὶ βοὴ θαλερῶν αἰζηῶν.
sentences.tr: meizōn dē para nēusi boē thalerōn aizēōn.
sentences.l: Greater now by the ships is the shout of flourishing vigorous young men.
sentences.i: The shout of the flourishing young men beside the ships is now greater.
sentences.n: No verb is written; supply ‘is’. μείζων is the comparative of μέγας ‘great’, with δή ‘now’, and βοή ‘shout’ is the subject, set against the ἰαχή of line 1. θαλερῶν αἰζηῶν ‘flourishing young men’ (αἰζηός is a vigorous young man in his prime) is a stock phrase for fighters; the Greek does not say which side.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ σὺ μὲν νῦν πῖνε καθήμενος αἴθοπα οἶνον
εἰς ὅ κε θερμὰ λοετρὰ ἐϋπλόκαμος Ἑκαμήδη
θερμήνῃ καὶ λούσῃ ἄπο βρότον αἱματόεντα·
sentences.tr:
alla sy men nyn pine kathēmenos aithopa oinon
eis ho ke therma loetra eÿplokamos Hekamēdē
thermēnēi kai lousēi apo broton haimatoenta·
sentences.i: But for now sit and drink the wine that has the look of fire, until fine-plaited Hecamede heats the warm baths and washes off the bloody gore;
sentences.n: ἀλλά ‘but’ sets Nestor’s order against the alarm. πῖνε is the present imperative of πίνω ‘drink’, and καθήμενος ‘sitting’ goes with it. εἰς ὅ κε with the aorist subjunctives θερμήνῃ and λούσῃ means ‘until she heats … and washes’. θερμὰ λοετρά, ‘the warm baths’, is the bath-water that Hecamede heats, and λούσῃ ἄπο is tmesis for ἀπολούσῃ ‘washes off’, with βρότον ‘gore’ as its object. ἐϋπλόκαμος ‘fine-plaited’ is Hecamede’s stock epithet, and αἴθοπα οἶνον, from αἴθω ‘burn’ and ὤψ ‘look’, is the wine that looks like fire.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ἐγὼν ἐλθὼν τάχα εἴσομαι ἐς περιωπήν.
sentences.tr: autar egōn elthōn tacha eisomai es periōpēn.
sentences.l: but I, having gone to a vantage-point, shall soon find out.”
sentences.i: But I shall go to a vantage-point and soon find out.”
sentences.n: αὐτάρ ‘but’ turns from Machaon to Nestor himself. ἐγών is the epic form of ἐγώ. ἐλθών ‘having gone’ takes ἐς περιωπήν, ‘to a vantage-point’, a place to look from. εἴσομαι is the future of οἶδα, ‘I shall know, find out’, and the Greek does not say what he will find out; τάχα means ‘soon’. The unit closes Nestor’s speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς εἰπὼν σάκος εἷλε τετυγμένον υἷος ἑοῖο
κείμενον ἐν κλισίῃ Θρασυμήδεος ἱπποδάμοιο
χαλκῷ παμφαῖνον·
sentences.tr:
hōs eipōn sakos heile tetygmenon huios heoio
keimenon en klisiēi Thrasymēdeos hippodamoio
chalkōi pamphainon·
sentences.i: So saying, he took his own son’s well-wrought shield, which lay in the hut of Thrasymedes, tamer of horses, gleaming all over with bronze;
sentences.n: ὣς εἰπών ‘so saying’ ends the speech and begins an action, with Nestor as the subject; εἷλε is the aorist of αἱρέω ‘take’. τετυγμένον ‘wrought’, κείμενον ‘lying’ and παμφαῖνον ‘gleaming all over’ (παν- + φαίνω) all agree with σάκος ‘shield’. υἷος ἑοῖο is ‘of his own son’: ἑοῖο is the possessive ὅς (epic genitive -οιο), not the pronoun. The son is Thrasymedes, in whose hut the shield lay; the next line shows him carrying Nestor’s own shield. κλισίῃ is ‘hut’, the house word, and ἱπποδάμοιο ‘horse-taming’ is a stock epithet. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line.

sentences.t: ὃ δ’ ἔχ’ ἀσπίδα πατρὸς ἑοῖο.
sentences.tr: ho d’ ech’ aspida patros heoio.
sentences.l: and he had the shield of his own father.
sentences.i: while he had his own father’s shield.
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ ‘and he’ is Thrasymedes, and ἔχ’ is the elided imperfect ἔχε, ‘he had’ (Attic εἶχεν), without the augment. ἀσπίδα is the other word for ‘shield’, where the line before had σάκος: Nestor and his son have each other’s shields. ἑοῖο is again the possessive, ‘his own father’s’, that is, Nestor’s. The unit begins in mid-line, after the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
εἵλετο δ’ ἄλκιμον ἔγχος ἀκαχμένον ὀξέϊ χαλκῷ,
στῆ δ’ ἐκτὸς κλισίης, τάχα δ’ εἴσιδεν ἔργον ἀεικὲς
τοὺς μὲν ὀρινομένους, τοὺς δὲ κλονέοντας ὄπισθε
Τρῶας ὑπερθύμους·
sentences.tr:
heileto d’ alkimon enchos akachmenon oxeï chalkōi,
stē d’ ektos klisiēs, tacha d’ eisiden ergon aeikes
tous men orinomenous, tous de kloneontas opisthe
Trōas hyperthymous·
sentences.l:
and he took up a sturdy spear, pointed with sharp bronze,
and stood outside the hut, and soon saw an unseemly deed,
some being stirred up, others throwing them into confusion from behind,
the high-spirited Trojans;
sentences.i: He took up a sturdy spear, pointed with sharp bronze, and stood outside the hut, and soon saw an unseemly deed: some stirred up, and others, the high-spirited Trojans, throwing them into confusion from behind;
sentences.n: The first line is a line of arming that stands elsewhere in the Iliad (10.135), and its English is kept. εἵλετο is the aorist middle of αἱρέω, ‘took for himself’; στῆ is the unaugmented aorist of ἵστημι, ‘stood’; εἴσιδεν is the aorist of εἰσοράω ‘catch sight of’. ἔργον ἀεικές is ‘an unseemly deed’, and the two accusatives that follow, τοὺς μὲν … τοὺς δέ ‘some … others’, say what it is: the ὀρινομένους ‘being stirred up’ are the Achaeans, as 59 will show, and the κλονέοντας ‘throwing into confusion’ are the Τρῶας ὑπερθύμους, the ‘high-spirited’ Trojans, named last.

sentences.t: ἐρέριπτο δὲ τεῖχος Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.tr: ereripto de teichos Achaiōn.
sentences.l: and had fallen down the wall of the Achaeans.
sentences.i: and the wall of the Achaeans had fallen down.
sentences.n: ἐρέριπτο is the pluperfect of ἐρείπω ‘throw down’ in its intransitive sense, ‘had fallen’, and τεῖχος ‘wall’ is its subject, held to the end of the clause. The wall is the one Nestor will speak of in 55–56 as the shelter of the ships. The unit begins in mid-line, after the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτε πορφύρῃ πέλαγος μέγα κύματι κωφῷ
ὀσσόμενον λιγέων ἀνέμων λαιψηρὰ κέλευθα
αὔτως, οὐδ’ ἄρα τε προκυλίνδεται οὐδετέρωσε,
πρίν τινα κεκριμένον καταβήμεναι ἐκ Διὸς οὖρον,
sentences.tr:
hōs d’ hote porphyrēi pelagos mega kymati kōphōi
ossomenon ligeōn anemōn laipsēra keleutha
autōs, oud’ ara te prokylindetai oudeterōse,
prin tina kekrimenon katabēmenai ek Dios ouron,
sentences.l:
And as when the great sea heaves darkly with a dull wave,
foreboding the quick ways of the clear winds,
just so, and does not roll forward either way,
before some decided wind has come down from Zeus,
sentences.i: As when the great sea heaves darkly with a dull wave, foreboding the quick ways of the clear-sounding winds, and just so rolls forward in neither direction, before a decided wind comes down from Zeus,
sentences.n: ὡς δ’ ὅτε ‘and as when’ opens a comparison that the ὣς at the start of line 20 closes. πορφύρῃ is the subjunctive of πορφύρω, said of the sea as it swells and darkens (compare πορφύρεον κῦμα ‘surging wave’, 1.482); κύματι κωφῷ is ‘with a dull wave’, a swell that makes no noise. ὀσσόμενον ‘foreboding’ agrees with πέλαγος ‘open sea’ and has the winds’ ‘quick ways’ as its object, and αὔτως is ‘just so’, in the same state. πρίν with the infinitive καταβήμεναι is ‘before … comes down’; κεκριμένον is a perfect passive participle of κρίνω ‘separate, decide’, so the wind is one that has been settled on.

sentences.t:
ὣς ὃ γέρων ὅρμαινε δαϊζόμενος κατὰ θυμὸν
διχθάδι’, ἢ μεθ’ ὅμιλον ἴοι Δαναῶν ταχυπώλων,
ἦε μετ’ Ἀτρεΐδην Ἀγαμέμνονα ποιμένα λαῶν.
sentences.tr:
hōs ho gerōn hormaine daïzomenos kata thymon
dichthadi’, ē meth’ homilon ioi Danaōn tachypōlōn,
ēe met’ Atreïdēn Agamemnona poimena laōn.
sentences.l:
So that old man pondered, torn in his heart
two ways, whether he should go among the throng of the swift-colted Danaans,
or go after Atreus’-son Agamemnon, shepherd of the people.
sentences.i: So the old man pondered, torn in his heart two ways: whether to go among the throng of the Danaans with their swift colts, or to go after Agamemnon, son of Atreus, shepherd of the people.
sentences.n: ὣς closes the comparison: the old man (ὃ γέρων, Nestor) is like the sea that swells but has not yet found its direction. ὅρμαινε is the imperfect of ὁρμαίνω ‘turn over in the mind’, and δαϊζόμενος is a participle of δαΐζω ‘tear apart’. διχθάδι’ is the neuter plural of διχθάδιος ‘twofold’ used as an adverb, ‘in two ways’. The first course is put as an optative, ἴοι, with ‘go’ understood after ἦε for the second: ‘whether he should go … or …’. Δαναῶν ταχυπώλων ‘of the Danaans with their swift colts’ and ποιμένα λαῶν ‘shepherd of the people’ are stock phrases, translated the same way every time.

sentences.t:
ὧδε δέ οἱ φρονέοντι δοάσσατο κέρδιον εἶναι
βῆναι ἐπ’ Ἀτρεΐδην.
sentences.tr:
hōde de hoi phroneonti doassato kerdion einai
bēnai ep’ Atreïdēn.
sentences.l:
And thus to him considering it seemed better to be
to go to Atreus’-son.
sentences.i: And this, as he thought it over, seemed to him the better course: to go to the son of Atreus.
sentences.n: The first line is the line that stands at 13.458, and its English is kept. φρονέοντι ‘considering’ is a dative participle agreeing with οἱ ‘to him’, and δοάσσατο is the aorist of δοάζομαι ‘seem’. κέρδιον is the comparative of κέρδος ‘gain’, ‘more advantageous, better’. Ἀτρεΐδην is Agamemnon, named in 22. The unit ends at the full stop in mid-line.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἀλλήλους ἐνάριζον
μαρνάμενοι·
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ allēlous enarizon
marnamenoi·
sentences.l:
And they slew one another
fighting;
sentences.i: And they were killing one another as they fought;
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ‘but they’ turns from Nestor’s thoughts to the fighting men. ἐνάριζον is the imperfect of ἐναρίζω; the verb properly means to strip a slain man of his arms, and in Homer it often stands simply for ‘kill’. μαρνάμενοι is the participle of μάρναμαι ‘fight’. The unit begins in mid-line, after the full stop, and ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
λάκε δέ σφι περὶ χροῒ χαλκὸς ἀτειρὴς
νυσσομένων ξίφεσίν τε καὶ ἔγχεσιν ἀμφιγύοισι.
sentences.tr:
lake de sphi peri chroï chalkos ateirēs
nyssomenōn xiphesin te kai enchesin amphigyoisi.
sentences.l:
and rang for them about the skin the unwearied bronze
of those being pierced with swords and with double-pointed spears.
sentences.i: and the unwearied bronze rang about their bodies as they were pierced with swords and double-pointed spears.
sentences.n: λάκε is the unaugmented aorist of λάσκω ‘ring, crash’, here of bronze; σφι ‘for them’ is a dative of the persons concerned, and χροῒ is the dative of χρώς ‘skin, body’, printed with the diaeresis. χαλκὸς ἀτειρής ‘the unwearied bronze’ is a stock phrase (ἀτειρής ‘not worn down’). The genitive νυσσομένων ‘of those being pierced’ names the men inside the bronze, loosely, as a genitive absolute does. The meaning of ἀμφιγύοισι is not known; ‘double-pointed’ is the usual guess and the house rendering.

sentences.t:
Νέστορι δὲ ξύμβληντο διοτρεφέες βασιλῆες
πὰρ νηῶν ἀνιόντες ὅσοι βεβλήατο χαλκῷ
Τυδεΐδης Ὀδυσεύς τε καὶ Ἀτρεΐδης Ἀγαμέμνων.
sentences.tr:
Nestori de xymblēnto diotrephees basilēes
par nēōn aniontes hosoi beblēato chalkōi
Tydeïdēs Odyseus te kai Atreïdēs Agamemnōn.
sentences.l:
And with Nestor met the Zeus-nurtured kings
coming up from beside the ships, as many as had been struck with bronze,
Tydeus’-son and Odysseus and Atreus’-son Agamemnon.
sentences.i: And Zeus-nurtured kings met Nestor, coming up from beside the ships, all who had been struck by bronze: the son of Tydeus, Odysseus, and Agamemnon, son of Atreus.
sentences.n: ξύμβληντο is the aorist middle of συμβάλλω in the sense ‘meet’, third plural, unaugmented, and takes the dative Νέστορι; the old spelling ξυν- stands for συν-. διοτρεφέες ‘Zeus-nurtured’ is the stock epithet of kings. ἀνιόντες ‘coming up’ is a participle of ἄνειμι, and ὅσοι βεβλήατο χαλκῷ, ‘as many as had been struck with bronze’, limits the kings to the wounded. The three are then named in apposition: Τυδεΐδης ‘son of Tydeus’ is Diomedes, whose own name is not given.

sentences.t:
πολλὸν γάρ ῥ’ ἀπάνευθε μάχης εἰρύατο νῆες
θῖν’ ἔφ’ ἁλὸς πολιῆς·
sentences.tr:
pollon gar rh’ apaneuthe machēs eiryato nēes
thin’ eph’ halos poliēs·
sentences.l:
For far apart from the fighting were drawn up the ships
on the shore of the grey sea;
sentences.i: For the ships were drawn up far from the fighting, on the shore of the grey sea;
sentences.n: γάρ ‘for’ opens an aside on where the ships lie. πολλὸν … ἀπάνευθε μάχης is ‘far apart from the fighting’, with the genitive of separation. εἰρύατο is the pluperfect passive of ἐρύω ‘draw’, third plural in the epic ending -ατο, ‘had been drawn up’. θῖν’ is θῖνα ‘shore’, ἔφ’ is ἐπί elided, and ἁλὸς πολιῆς is ‘of the grey sea’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line, and the aside goes on.

sentences.t:
τὰς γὰρ πρώτας πεδίον δὲ
εἴρυσαν, αὐτὰρ τεῖχος ἐπὶ πρύμνῃσιν ἔδειμαν.
sentences.tr:
tas gar prōtas pedion de
eirysan, autar teichos epi prymnēisin edeiman.
sentences.l:
for the first ones to the plain
they drew up, and then a wall by the sterns they built.
sentences.i: for they drew the first ships up on to the plain, and then built a wall at their sterns.
sentences.n: τὰς … πρώτας ‘the first ones’ are ships, and πεδίον δέ is ‘to the plain’, with the suffix -δε of direction. εἴρυσαν is the aorist of ἐρύω ‘draw’ with its augment (εἰ- for ἐ-ἐ-), and ἔδειμαν the aorist of δέμω ‘build’, also augmented. αὐτάρ ‘and then’ brings the wall, built ἐπὶ πρύμνῃσιν ‘by the sterns’ of those first ships. The unit begins in mid-line, after the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
οὐδὲ γὰρ οὐδ’ εὐρύς περ ἐὼν ἐδυνήσατο πάσας
αἰγιαλὸς νῆας χαδέειν, στείνοντο δὲ λαοί·
sentences.tr:
oude gar oud’ eurys per eōn edynēsato pasas
aigialos nēas chadeein, steinonto de laoi·
sentences.l:
For not even, wide though it was, was able all
the beach to hold the ships, and the people were crowded;
sentences.i: For the beach, wide though it was, could not hold all the ships, and the people were crowded;
sentences.n: οὐδὲ γὰρ οὐδ’ ‘for not even’ doubles the negative for emphasis. εὐρύς περ ἐὼν ‘wide though it was’ is a concessive participle phrase that belongs to αἰγιαλός ‘beach’, the subject of ἐδυνήσατο, held back to the next line; πάσας agrees with νῆας, ‘all the ships’. χαδέειν is the epic infinitive of χανδάνω ‘hold, contain’, and στείνοντο ‘were crowded’ is the unaugmented imperfect of στείνομαι. αἰγιαλός and ἠϊών (35) are both ‘beach’.

sentences.t:
τώ ῥα προκρόσσας ἔρυσαν, καὶ πλῆσαν ἁπάσης
ἠϊόνος στόμα μακρόν, ὅσον συνεέργαθον ἄκραι.
sentences.tr:
tō rha prokrossas erysan, kai plēsan hapasēs
ēïonos stoma makron, hoson syneergathon akrai.
sentences.l:
So in tiers they drew them, and filled of the whole
beach the long mouth, as far as the headlands shut it in.
sentences.i: So they drew them up in tiers and filled the long mouth of the whole beach, as far as the headlands shut it in.
sentences.n: τώ ῥα ‘so then’ (τῷ, ‘therefore’) leads to what they did. προκρόσσας is a rare word whose exact sense is not certain; ‘in tiers’, ships drawn up in rows one behind another, is the usual guess. ἔρυσαν and πλῆσαν are unaugmented aorists. ἠϊόνος στόμα μακρόν ‘the long mouth of the beach’ is the open front of the shore, and ὅσον ‘as far as’ goes with συνεέργαθον, the aorist of συνέργω ‘shut in together’, with ἄκραι ‘headlands’ as subject.

sentences.t:
τώ ῥ’ οἵ γ’ ὀψείοντες ἀϋτῆς καὶ πολέμοιο
ἔγχει ἐρειδόμενοι κίον ἀθρόοι·
sentences.tr:
tō rh’ hoi g’ opseiontes aÿtēs kai polemoio
enchei ereidomenoi kion athrooi·
sentences.l:
So they, wishing to see the battle-cry and war,
leaning on a spear, went all together;
sentences.i: So they went all together, leaning on their spears, wishing to look on the battle-cry and the war;
sentences.n: τώ ῥ’ οἵ γ’ ‘so they’ picks up the kings of 27–29. ὀψείοντες is a desiderative participle of ὄψομαι ‘I shall see’, ‘wishing to see’, and takes the genitives ἀϋτῆς καὶ πολέμοιο: they go to look on the fighting. ἔγχει ἐρειδόμενοι is ‘leaning on a spear’, a dative singular for the spear each man carries, and ἀθρόοι is ‘all together’. κίον is the unaugmented imperfect of κίω ‘go’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line.

sentences.t:
ἄχνυτο δέ σφι
θυμὸς ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν.
sentences.tr:
achnyto de sphi
thymos eni stēthessin.
sentences.l:
and was grieved for them
the heart in their breasts.
sentences.i: and the heart in their breasts was grieved.
sentences.n: ἄχνυτο is the unaugmented imperfect middle of ἄχνυμαι ‘be troubled, grieve’, and σφι ‘for them’ is the dative of the persons affected. θυμός is ‘heart’, the seat of feeling, and ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν ‘in their breasts’ has the epic dative plural -εσσι(ν). The unit begins in mid-line, after the ano teleia, and ends at the full stop.

sentences.t:
ὃ δὲ ξύμβλητο γεραιὸς
Νέστωρ, πτῆξε δὲ θυμὸν ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.tr:
ho de xymblēto geraios
Nestōr, ptēxe de thymon eni stēthessin Achaiōn.
sentences.l:
And he met (them), the old man
Nestor, and made cower the heart in the breasts of the Achaeans.
sentences.i: Old Nestor met them, and made the heart in the breasts of the Achaeans cower.
sentences.n: ὃ δὲ ‘and he’ is Nestor, named after γεραιός ‘old’, and ξύμβλητο is the third singular of the same aorist as ξύμβληντο in 27, unaugmented; the kings he meets are not repeated. πτῆξε is an aorist of πτήσσω ‘cower’. It is usually intransitive, but here it has the object θυμόν, and the unit takes it as ‘made cower’: Nestor’s coming away from the fighting dismays the army. The Greek could also be read ‘cowered in heart’; Ἀχαιῶν is probably the whole army, since the kings are named apart in 27–29. The unit begins in mid-line.

sentences.t: τὸν καὶ φωνήσας προσέφη κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων·
sentences.tr: ton kai phōnēsas prosephē kreiōn Agamemnōn·
sentences.l: And him, lifting his voice, addressed lord Agamemnon:
sentences.i: And lord Agamemnon lifted his voice and spoke to him:
sentences.n: The line is a stock introduction to a speech. τὸν is the pronoun ‘him’, Nestor; φωνήσας ‘lifting his voice’ is an aorist participle of φωνέω, and προσέφη ‘addressed’ is the past tense of πρόσφημι, with its augment. κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων ‘lord Agamemnon’ is the stock phrase, the subject, held to the end.

sentences.t:
ὦ Νέστορ Νηληϊάδη μέγα κῦδος Ἀχαιῶν
τίπτε λιπὼν πόλεμον φθισήνορα δεῦρ’ ἀφικάνεις;
sentences.tr:
ō Nestor Nēlēïadē mega kydos Achaiōn
tipte lipōn polemon phthisēnora deur’ aphikaneis;
sentences.l:
“O Nestor, son of Neleus, great glory of the Achaeans,
why, leaving the man-wasting war, here do you come?
sentences.i: “Nestor, son of Neleus, great glory of the Achaeans, why have you left the war that wastes men and come here?
sentences.n: The first line is the line that stands at 10.87, and its English is kept. Νηληϊάδη is a patronymic, ‘son of Neleus’, and μέγα κῦδος Ἀχαιῶν ‘great glory of the Achaeans’ is in apposition to the vocative. τίπτε is ‘why’ (= τί ποτε), and λιπών is the aorist participle of λείπω ‘leave’. πόλεμον φθισήνορα ‘man-wasting war’ is formed from φθίω ‘waste’ and ἀνήρ ‘man’; the house rendering is kept. ἀφικάνεις is the present of ἀφικάνω ‘arrive’, and δεῦρ’ is ‘here’.

sentences.t:
δείδω μὴ δή μοι τελέσῃ ἔπος ὄβριμος Ἕκτωρ,
ὥς ποτ’ ἐπηπείλησεν ἐνὶ Τρώεσσ’ ἀγορεύων
μὴ πρὶν πὰρ νηῶν προτὶ Ἴλιον ἀπονέεσθαι
πρὶν πυρὶ νῆας ἐνιπρῆσαι, κτεῖναι δὲ καὶ αὐτούς.
sentences.tr:
deidō mē dē moi telesēi epos obrimos Hektōr,
hōs pot’ epēpeilēsen eni Trōess’ agoreuōn
mē prin par nēōn proti Ilion aponeesthai
prin pyri nēas eniprēsai, kteinai de kai autous.
sentences.l:
I fear lest indeed to me mighty Hector fulfil his word,
as once he threatened, speaking among the Trojans,
that not before from the ships to Ilios would he go back
before with fire the ships he should set ablaze, and kill the men themselves.
sentences.i: I fear that mighty Hector may now fulfil to my cost the word he once threatened, speaking among the Trojans: that he would not go back from the ships to Ilios until he had set the ships on fire and killed the men themselves.
sentences.n: δείδω μή … τελέσῃ is a fear clause, μή with the subjunctive, ‘I fear lest he fulfil’, and μοι is ‘to my cost’. ὄβριμος ‘mighty’ is Hector’s stock epithet. ὥς ποτ’ ἐπηπείλησεν ‘as he once threatened’ introduces the threat, which is put in infinitives with μή: ἀπονέεσθαι ‘go back’, ἐνιπρῆσαι ‘set on fire’, κτεῖναι ‘kill’. Τρώεσσ’ is the epic dative plural, and αὐτούς ‘the men themselves’ are set against the ships. The sentence is four lines long and has its stop only at the end.

sentences.t: κεῖνος τὼς ἀγόρευε·
sentences.tr: keinos tōs agoreue·
sentences.l: That man thus was speaking;
sentences.i: That is how he spoke;
sentences.n: κεῖνος is the epic form of ἐκεῖνος ‘that man’, Hector, and τώς is ὥς ‘so’. ἀγόρευε is the unaugmented imperfect of ἀγορεύω ‘speak out’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line.

sentences.t: τὰ δὴ νῦν πάντα τελεῖται.
sentences.tr: ta dē nyn panta teleitai.
sentences.l: these things now all are being fulfilled.
sentences.i: and now all of it is being fulfilled.
sentences.n: τὰ is the pronoun ‘these things’ (the same line stands at 2.330, with the same English), and τελεῖται is the present passive of τελέω ‘fulfil’, the verb of τελέσῃ in 44. The unit begins in mid-line, after the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
ὢ πόποι ἦ ῥα καὶ ἄλλοι ἐϋκνήμιδες Ἀχαιοὶ
ἐν θυμῷ βάλλονται ἐμοὶ χόλον ὥς περ Ἀχιλλεὺς
οὐδ’ ἐθέλουσι μάχεσθαι ἐπὶ πρυμνῇσι νέεσσι.
sentences.tr:
ō popoi ē rha kai alloi eÿknēmides Achaioi
en thymōi ballontai emoi cholon hōs per Achilleus
oud’ ethelousi machesthai epi prymnēisi neessi.
sentences.l:
Ah, truly then the other well-greaved Achaeans too
in their heart lay up anger against me, just as Achilles,
and are not willing to fight at the sterns of the ships.”
sentences.i: Ah, so the other well-greaved Achaeans too bear anger against me in their hearts, just as Achilles does, and are unwilling to fight at the sterns of the ships.”
sentences.n: ὢ πόποι ‘Ah!’ opens the cry (the house rendering), and ἦ ῥα is ‘truly then’. ἐν θυμῷ βάλλονται … χόλον is ‘lay up anger in the heart’, βάλλομαι being the middle, ‘put for oneself’, with ἐμοί ‘against me’; ὥς περ Ἀχιλλεύς has its verb understood. ἐϋκνήμιδες ‘well-greaved’ is the stock epithet, and ἐπὶ πρυμνῇσι νέεσσι has the epic dative plurals -ῃσι and -εσσι, ‘at the sterns of the ships’. The unit closes Agamemnon’s speech.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα Γερήνιος ἱππότα Νέστωρ·
sentences.tr: ton d’ ēmeibet’ epeita Gerēnios hippota Nestōr·
sentences.l: Him then answered the Gerenian horseman Nestor:
sentences.i: Then the Gerenian horseman Nestor answered him:
sentences.n: The reply formula, as at 4.317: τόν ‘him’ is Agamemnon, ἠμείβετο ‘answered’, ἔπειτα ‘then’. Γερήνιος ἱππότα is Nestor’s stock name-epithet; ἱππότα is an old nominative in -ᾱ (= ἱππότης), and the meaning of Γερήνιος is disputed, so the English leaves it as a name. A new paragraph begins at 52.

sentences.t:
ἦ δὴ ταῦτά γ’ ἑτοῖμα τετεύχαται, οὐδέ κεν ἄλλως
Ζεὺς ὑψιβρεμέτης αὐτὸς παρατεκτήναιτο.
sentences.tr:
ē dē tauta g’ hetoima teteuchatai, oude ken allōs
Zeus hypsibremetēs autos paratektēnaito.
sentences.l:
“Truly indeed these things at least have been made ready, nor in any other way
would Zeus the high-thundering himself rework them.
sentences.i: “Truly, these things have been made ready, and not even Zeus himself, who thunders on high, could alter them.
sentences.n: ἦ δή ‘truly indeed’ stresses the claim. ἑτοῖμα τετεύχαται is the perfect passive of τεύχω ‘make’ in the epic third plural -αται, ‘have been made ready’: what Agamemnon fears is already in place. οὐδέ κεν ἄλλως … παρατεκτήναιτο is a potential optative, ‘nor could … in any other way …’. παρατεκτήναιτο is built on τέκτων ‘carpenter’ and here means ‘rework, alter’; the Odyssey (14.131) uses it of making up a story, and its exact sense here is not certain. Ζεὺς ὑψιβρεμέτης is the house ‘Zeus who thunders on high’.

sentences.t:
τεῖχος μὲν γὰρ δὴ κατερήριπεν, ᾧ ἐπέπιθμεν
ἄρρηκτον νηῶν τε καὶ αὐτῶν εἶλαρ ἔσεσθαι·
sentences.tr:
teichos men gar dē katerēripen, hōi epepithmen
arrēkton nēōn te kai autōn eilar esesthai·
sentences.l:
For the wall has fallen down, in which we trusted
unbreakable of the ships and of ourselves a shelter to be;
sentences.i: for the wall has fallen down, the wall in which we trusted that it would be an unbreakable shelter for the ships and for ourselves;
sentences.n: κατερήριπεν is the perfect of κατερείπω in its intransitive sense, ‘has fallen down’, as ἐρέριπτο at 15. ἐπέπιθμεν is the pluperfect of πείθομαι ‘trust’, epic first plural in -μεν, ‘we had trusted’; it takes the dative ᾧ and the infinitive ἔσεσθαι. ἄρρηκτον … εἶλαρ is ‘an unbreakable shelter’, and νηῶν τε καὶ αὐτῶν ‘of the ships and of the men themselves’. The second line stands word for word at 68, in Agamemnon’s mouth, and its English is the same.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἐπὶ νηυσὶ θοῇσι μάχην ἀλίαστον ἔχουσι
νωλεμές·
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ epi nēusi thoēisi machēn aliaston echousi
nōlemes·
sentences.l:
and they at the swift ships a relentless fight keep up
unceasingly;
sentences.i: and they are keeping up a relentless fight at the swift ships, unceasingly;
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ‘but they’ are the fighters at the ships. μάχην ἔχουσι is ‘they keep up the fight’, ἀλίαστον ‘relentless’ is the stock word for war, and νωλεμές ‘unceasingly’ is an adverb. νηυσὶ θοῇσι has the epic dative plurals -υσι and -ῃσι, ‘the swift ships’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἂν ἔτι γνοίης μάλα περ σκοπιάζων
ὁπποτέρωθεν Ἀχαιοὶ ὀρινόμενοι κλονέονται,
ὡς ἐπιμὶξ κτείνονται, ἀϋτὴ δ’ οὐρανὸν ἵκει.
sentences.tr:
oud’ an eti gnoiēs mala per skopiazōn
hoppoterōthen Achaioi orinomenoi kloneontai,
hōs epimix kteinontai, aÿtē d’ ouranon hikei.
sentences.i: and you could no longer tell, however closely you watched, from which side the Achaeans are being stirred up and thrown into confusion, so mixed together are they killed, and the cry reaches heaven.
sentences.n: οὐδ’ ἂν ἔτι γνοίης is a potential optative, ‘you could no longer tell’, with ‘you’ meaning anyone; μάλα περ σκοπιάζων is ‘however closely you watched’ (σκοπιάζω ‘spy out’). ὁπποτέρωθεν ‘from which of two sides’ introduces an indirect question, and ὀρινόμενοι κλονέονται ‘are stirred up, are thrown into confusion’ takes up the Achaeans’ state at 14 and 15. ἐπιμίξ is ‘in a mixed mass’, and ἀϋτὴ δ’ οὐρανὸν ἵκει ‘and the cry reaches heaven’ echoes 2.153, ἀϋτὴ δ’ οὐρανὸν ἷκεν. The unit begins in mid-line, after the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
ἡμεῖς δὲ φραζώμεθ’ ὅπως ἔσται τάδε ἔργα
εἴ τι νόος ῥέξει·
sentences.tr:
hēmeis de phrazōmeth’ hopōs estai tade erga
ei ti noos rhexei·
sentences.l:
But let us ourselves consider how these deeds shall be,
if mind will do anything;
sentences.i: But let us consider how these things are to turn out, and whether our minds can do anything;
sentences.n: φραζώμεθ’ is a subjunctive of exhortation, ‘let us consider’, with ὅπως ἔσται ‘how it will be’. The line stands also at 4.14, and Nestor has used the same words in the imperative at 3. εἴ τι νόος ῥέξει is ‘if mind will do anything’, with νόος ‘mind’ as subject and ῥέξει the future of ῥέζω ‘do’; after ‘consider’ it asks whether thinking can achieve something. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line.

sentences.t:
πόλεμον δ’ οὐκ ἄμμε κελεύω
δύμεναι·
sentences.tr:
polemon d’ ouk amme keleuō
dymenai·
sentences.l:
but into war I do not bid us
to go;
sentences.i: but I do not urge us to go into the war;
sentences.n: πόλεμον … δύμεναι: δύμεναι is the epic infinitive of δύω ‘enter, plunge into’, with πόλεμον the place entered (compare μάχην καταδύμεναι, 3.241). ἄμμε is the epic ‘us’ (= ἡμᾶς), the subject of the infinitive, and κελεύω is ‘I bid, urge’. The unit begins in mid-line and ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t: οὐ γάρ πως βεβλημένον ἐστὶ μάχεσθαι.
sentences.tr: ou gar pōs beblēmenon esti machesthai.
sentences.l: for in no way, one who has been struck, is it possible to fight.”
sentences.i: for it is in no way possible to fight when one is wounded.”
sentences.n: οὐ γάρ πως ‘for in no way’ gives the reason. βεβλημένον is a perfect passive participle, ‘one who has been struck’, the unstated subject of μάχεσθαι; ἐστί with the infinitive means ‘it is possible’. The unit closes Nestor’s speech. The kings he has met are all wounded.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπεν ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγαμέμνων·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aute proseeipen anax andrōn Agamemnōn·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed the lord of men, Agamemnon:
sentences.i: Then Agamemnon, lord of men, spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: The formula for a speaker who answers in turn, as at 9.114: τὸν is the pronoun ‘him’, αὖτε ‘in turn’, and προσέειπεν the Homeric form of ‘addressed’ (Attic προσεῖπε), kept apart from ἠμείβετο ‘answered’. ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν ‘lord of men’ is Agamemnon’s stock title. A new paragraph begins at 64.

sentences.t:
Νέστορ ἐπεὶ δὴ νηυσὶν ἔπι πρυμνῇσι μάχονται,
τεῖχος δ’ οὐκ ἔχραισμε τετυγμένον, οὐδέ τι τάφρος,
ᾗ ἔπι πολλὰ πάθον Δαναοί, ἔλποντο δὲ θυμῷ
ἄρρηκτον νηῶν τε καὶ αὐτῶν εἶλαρ ἔσεσθαι·
sentences.tr:
Nestor epei dē nēusin epi prymnēisi machontai,
teichos d’ ouk echraisme tetygmenon, oude ti taphros,
hēi epi polla pathon Danaoi, elponto de thymōi
arrēkton nēōn te kai autōn eilar esesthai·
sentences.l:
“Nestor, since now at the ships by the sterns they fight,
and the wall did not help, wrought as it was, nor at all the ditch,
for which the Danaans suffered many things, and hoped in their heart
unbreakable of the ships and of ourselves a shelter to be;
sentences.i: “Nestor, since they are now fighting at the ships by their sterns, and the well-wrought wall did not help, nor did the ditch, for which the Danaans suffered much; and they hoped in their hearts that there would be an unbreakable shelter for the ships and for ourselves;
sentences.n: ἐπεὶ δή ‘since indeed’ opens a reason clause whose main clause comes only at 69, so that the conclusion is held back. νηυσὶν ἔπι πρυμνῇσι is ἐπὶ νηυσὶ πρυμνῇσι with the preposition after its noun, ‘at the ships’ sterns’. ἔχραισμε is the aorist of χραισμέω ‘avail, help’, and the verb is understood with οὐδέ τι τάφρος ‘nor at all the ditch’. τετυγμένον ‘wrought’ agrees with τεῖχος. ᾗ is feminine and so refers to the ditch, with ἔπι after it: ‘for which’. ἔλποντο is the imperfect of ἔλπομαι ‘hope’ with the infinitive ἔσεσθαι. The last line is Nestor’s line 56 again, and the English is the same.

sentences.t:
οὕτω που Διὶ μέλλει ὑπερμενέϊ φίλον εἶναι
νωνύμνους ἀπολέσθαι ἀπ’ Ἄργεος ἐνθάδ’ Ἀχαιούς.
sentences.tr:
houtō pou Dii mellei hypermeneï philon einai
nōnymnous apolesthai ap’ Argeos enthad’ Achaious.
sentences.l:
So, I suppose, to Zeus exceeding-strong it is likely to be dear
nameless to perish far from Argos here the Achaeans.
sentences.i: So, I suppose, it is bound to be dear to Zeus of surpassing strength that the Achaeans perish here, nameless, far from Argos.
sentences.n: The main clause at last: οὕτω που … μέλλει … φίλον εἶναι ‘so, I suppose, it is bound to be dear’, with Διὶ ὑπερμενέϊ ‘to Zeus of surpassing strength’ and the infinitive ἀπολέσθαι ‘to perish’ as what is dear to him. νωνύμνους ‘nameless’ and ἀπ’ Ἄργεος ‘far from Argos’ describe the Achaeans’ death. The two lines stand also at 2.116 and 12.70, and their English is kept.

sentences.t:
ᾔδεα μὲν γὰρ ὅτε πρόφρων Δαναοῖσιν ἄμυνεν,
οἶδα δὲ νῦν ὅτε τοὺς μὲν ὁμῶς μακάρεσσι θεοῖσι
κυδάνει, ἡμέτερον δὲ μένος καὶ χεῖρας ἔδησεν.
sentences.tr:
ēidea men gar hote prophrōn Danaoisin amynen,
oida de nyn hote tous men homōs makaressi theoisi
kydanei, hēmeteron de menos kai cheiras edēsen.
sentences.l:
For I knew when ready-minded he warded off for the Danaans,
and I know now that these on a level with the blessed gods
he gives glory to, and our strength and hands he has bound.
sentences.i: For I knew it when he warded off harm from the Danaans with a ready mind, and I know now that he gives glory to these men on a level with the blessed gods, and has bound our strength and our hands.
sentences.n: ᾔδεα is the pluperfect of οἶδα, ‘I knew’, against οἶδα ‘I know’ in the next line; ὅτε is ‘when’ the first time and perhaps ‘that’ the second, which the Greek leaves open. ἄμυνεν ‘warded off’ takes the dative Δαναοῖσιν, ‘for the Danaans’; the thing warded off is not said, and the English supplies ‘harm’. πρόφρων is the house ‘ready-minded’. τοὺς μέν ‘these’ are the Trojans, not named, set against ἡμέτερον … μένος ‘our strength’. ὁμῶς + dative is ‘on a level with’, κυδάνει is κυδαίνει ‘gives glory to’, and ἔδησεν is the aorist ‘has bound’.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγεθ’ ὡς ἂν ἐγὼν εἴπω πειθώμεθα πάντες.
sentences.tr: all’ ageth’ hōs an egōn eipō peithōmetha pantes.
sentences.l: But come, as I may say let us obey, all of us.
sentences.i: But come, let us all do as I say.
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγεθ’ ‘but come’ is ἄγετε with elision. ὡς ἂν … εἴπω is an aorist subjunctive with ἄν, ‘as I shall say’, and πειθώμεθα is the subjunctive of exhortation of πείθομαι ‘obey’, which takes an unstated dative ‘me’. ἐγών is the epic form of ἐγώ.

sentences.t:
νῆες ὅσαι πρῶται εἰρύαται ἄγχι θαλάσσης
ἕλκωμεν, πάσας δὲ ἐρύσσομεν εἰς ἅλα δῖαν,
sentences.tr:
nēes hosai prōtai eiryatai anchi thalassēs
helkōmen, pasas de eryssomen eis hala dian,
sentences.l:
The ships as many as first are drawn up near the sea
let us haul, and all let us drag into the heavenly brine,
sentences.i: As for the foremost ships, all that are drawn up near the sea, let us haul them, and drag them all into the heavenly brine,
sentences.n: νῆες ὅσαι ‘the ships as many as’ is a nominative left standing at the head of the sentence; ἕλκωμεν (the subjunctive of exhortation of ἕλκω ‘haul’) takes them as its object in sense, and πάσας ‘all of them’ picks them up in the accusative. εἰρύαται is the perfect passive of ἐρύω with the epic ending -αται, ‘are drawn up’. πρῶται ‘first’ is here a place in the line, the ships nearest the sea, as ἄγχι θαλάσσης shows; the English says ‘foremost’. ἐρύσσομεν is another subjunctive, of ἐρύω ‘drag’. ἅλα δῖαν is ‘the heavenly brine’, as at 2.140, δῖος keeping its house rendering even of the sea.

sentences.t:
ὕψι δ’ ἐπ’ εὐνάων ὁρμίσσομεν, εἰς ὅ κεν ἔλθῃ
νὺξ ἀβρότη, ἢν καὶ τῇ ἀπόσχωνται πολέμοιο
Τρῶες·
sentences.tr:
hypsi d’ ep’ eunaōn hormissomen, eis ho ken elthēi
nyx abrotē, ēn kai tēi aposchōntai polemoio
Trōes·
sentences.i: and moor them afloat on anchor-stones until immortal night comes, if the Trojans will hold back from the war even so;
sentences.n: ὕψι ‘high’, with εὐνάων, the ‘beds’ that serve as anchor-stones, probably means ships riding at anchor off the ground, afloat; ὁρμίσσομεν is the subjunctive of ὁρμίζω ‘moor’. εἰς ὅ κεν ἔλθῃ is ‘until there comes’. ἀβρότη is ἀ- + βροτός, ‘immortal, divine’, said of night. ἢν καὶ τῇ ἀπόσχωνται πολέμοιο is ‘if even so they hold back from the war’: ἀπέχομαι takes the genitive, and the force of τῇ (‘so, in that way’, or ‘there’) is not certain. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line.

sentences.t: ἔπειτα δέ κεν ἐρυσαίμεθα νῆας ἁπάσας.
sentences.tr: epeita de ken erysaimetha nēas hapasas.
sentences.l: and then we could drag all the ships.
sentences.i: and then we could drag all the ships.
sentences.n: ἔπειτα δέ κεν ἐρυσαίμεθα is a potential, ‘and then we could drag’, the aorist optative middle of ἐρύω with κεν. νῆας ἁπάσας ‘all the ships’ goes beyond the foremost ones of 75. The unit begins in mid-line, after the ano teleia.

sentences.t: οὐ γάρ τις νέμεσις φυγέειν κακόν, οὐδ’ ἀνὰ νύκτα.
sentences.tr: ou gar tis nemesis phygeein kakon, oud’ ana nykta.
sentences.l: For not any resentment is it to flee evil, not even by night.
sentences.i: For it is no cause for resentment to flee from evil, even at night.
sentences.n: νέμεσις ‘resentment’ is the blame another man’s act arouses; there is no verb, ‘is’ being understood, and οὐ … τις makes it ‘not any’. φυγέειν is the epic infinitive of φεύγω, and κακόν ‘evil’ is its object. οὐδ’ ἀνὰ νύκτα is ‘not even through the night’: flight under cover of dark is no shame.

sentences.t: βέλτερον ὃς φεύγων προφύγῃ κακὸν ἠὲ ἁλώῃ.
sentences.tr: belteron hos pheugōn prophygēi kakon ēe halōēi.
sentences.l: Better whoever, fleeing, escapes evil, than is caught.”
sentences.i: It is better that a man should flee and escape evil than be caught.”
sentences.n: βέλτερον ‘better’ is the epic comparative of ἀγαθός. ὃς φεύγων προφύγῃ is a general relative clause with the aorist subjunctive of προφεύγω ‘escape’, and ἠέ ‘than’ introduces the second subjunctive ἁλώῃ, the aorist of ἁλίσκομαι ‘be caught’. The unit closes Agamemnon’s speech.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἄρ’ ὑπόδρα ἰδὼν προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.tr: ton d’ ar’ hypodra idōn prosephē polymētis Odysseus·
sentences.l: Him then with a scowl looking addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: Then Odysseus of many wiles, looking at him with a scowl, spoke to him:
sentences.n: τὸν δ’ ἄρ’ ‘and him then’ is Agamemnon. ὑπόδρα ἰδών ‘looking with a scowl’ is the stock look of anger or reproach; ‘from under the brows’ is the ancient explanation of ὑπόδρα, but its derivation is not certain. προσέφη ‘addressed’ and πολύμητις ‘of many wiles’ are as in the line at 4.349, which this is. A new paragraph begins at 82.

sentences.t: Ἀτρεΐδη ποῖόν σε ἔπος φύγεν ἕρκος ὀδόντων;
sentences.tr: Atreïdē poion se epos phygen herkos odontōn;
sentences.l: “Atreus’-son, what sort of word has escaped you, (past) the fence of your teeth?
sentences.i: “Son of Atreus, what kind of word has slipped past the fence of your teeth?
sentences.n: Odysseus answers with a vocative, Ἀτρεΐδη ‘son of Atreus’, and a question that is a charge. ποῖον ‘what sort of’ goes with ἔπος ‘word’, and φύγεν is the aorist of φεύγω ‘escape’ without its augment (= ἔφυγε), with σε ‘you’ as its object; ἕρκος ὀδόντων ‘the fence of the teeth’ is what the word passes. The line stands also at 4.350, and its English is kept.

sentences.t:
οὐλόμεν’ αἴθ’ ὤφελλες ἀεικελίου στρατοῦ ἄλλου
σημαίνειν, μὴ δ’ ἄμμιν ἀνασσέμεν, οἷσιν ἄρα Ζεὺς
ἐκ νεότητος ἔδωκε καὶ ἐς γῆρας τολυπεύειν
ἀργαλέους πολέμους, ὄφρα φθιόμεσθα ἕκαστος.
sentences.tr:
oulomen’ aith’ ōphelles aeikeliou stratou allou
sēmainein, mē d’ ammin anassemen, hoisin ara Zeus
ek neotētos edōke kai es gēras tolypeuein
argaleous polemous, ophra phthiomestha hekastos.
sentences.l:
Ruinous one, would that of some other, unseemly army
you were in command, and not ruling over us, to whom indeed Zeus
from youth has given, and into old age, to wind off
grievous wars, until we perish, each one.
sentences.i: You ruinous man, would that you were in command of some other, unseemly army, and not ruling over us, to whom Zeus has given, from youth into old age, to wind grievous wars to their end, until each one of us perishes.
sentences.n: οὐλόμεν’ is the vocative of οὐλόμενος, the participle of ὄλλυμι used as an adjective and as a curse-word, ‘you ruinous man’. αἴθ’ ὤφελλες … σημαίνειν is a wish that cannot now be met: αἴθε ‘would that’ with the imperfect of ὀφείλω and an infinitive. σημαίνειν ‘to command’ takes the genitive στρατοῦ ἄλλου, and ἀεικελίου is ‘unseemly’. ἀνασσέμεν is the epic infinitive of ἀνάσσω ‘rule over’, with the dative ἄμμιν ‘us’. τολυπεύειν is a wool-working word, ‘wind off to the end’, used of working through wars; ὄφρα φθιόμεσθα is a short-vowel subjunctive, ‘until we perish’.

sentences.t:
οὕτω δὴ μέμονας Τρώων πόλιν εὐρυάγυιαν
καλλείψειν, ἧς εἵνεκ’ ὀϊζύομεν κακὰ πολλά;
sentences.tr:
houtō dē memonas Trōōn polin euryaguian
kalleipsein, hēs heinek’ oïzyomen kaka polla;
sentences.l:
So indeed are you set the city of the Trojans, wide-streeted,
to leave behind, for whose sake we suffer many evils?
sentences.i: Are you really so set on abandoning the city of the Trojans, with its wide streets, for whose sake we suffer so many evils?
sentences.n: μέμονας is a perfect with present sense, ‘you are eager, set on’, and takes the infinitive καλλείψειν, an epic form of καταλείψειν ‘leave behind’. εὐρυάγυιαν ‘of the wide streets’ is the house word for Troy’s epithet. ἧς εἵνεκ’ is ‘for whose sake’, with the relative in the genitive, and ὀϊζύομεν κακὰ πολλά ‘we suffer many evils’ has ὀϊζύω ‘suffer woe’ (related to ὀϊζύς ‘distress’) and κακά as an internal accusative. The question ends at the Greek question mark.

sentences.t:
σίγα, μή τίς τ’ ἄλλος Ἀχαιῶν τοῦτον ἀκούσῃ
μῦθον, ὃν οὔ κεν ἀνήρ γε διὰ στόμα πάμπαν ἄγοιτο
ὅς τις ἐπίσταιτο ᾗσι φρεσὶν ἄρτια βάζειν
σκηπτοῦχός τ’ εἴη,
sentences.tr:
siga, mē tis t’ allos Achaiōn touton akousēi
mython, hon ou ken anēr ge dia stoma pampan agoito
hos tis epistaito hēisi phresin artia bazein
skēptouchos t’ eiē,
sentences.l:
Be silent, lest some other of the Achaeans hear this
word, which no man at all would bring through his mouth,
whoever knew in his own wits how to speak what is fitting
and were a sceptre-bearer,
sentences.i: Be silent, lest some other of the Achaeans hear this word, which no man would ever utter, no man who knew in his own mind how to speak what is fitting and was a sceptre-bearer,
sentences.n: σίγα is the imperative of σιγάω ‘be silent’, and μή … ἀκούσῃ is ‘lest he hear’, with the aorist subjunctive. ὃν οὔ κεν … ἄγοιτο is a potential optative: ἄγοιτο is the middle of ἄγω, ‘would bring out’, and διὰ στόμα ‘through the mouth’, so ‘would utter’. ὅς τις ἐπίσταιτο is ‘whoever knew how’; ᾗσι φρεσίν is ‘in his own wits’ (ᾗσι is the possessive ὅς in the epic dative plural, not a relative), and ἄρτια is ‘what is fitting’. Line 92 is also Odyssey 8.240, and its English is kept. σκηπτοῦχος ‘sceptre-bearer’ is the king’s mark.

sentences.t:
καί οἱ πειθοίατο λαοὶ
τοσσοίδ’ ὅσσοισιν σὺ μετ’ Ἀργείοισιν ἀνάσσεις·
sentences.tr:
kai hoi peithoiato laoi
tossoid’ hossoisin sy met’ Argeioisin anasseis·
sentences.l:
and to him would be obedient the people
as many as those over whom you rule among the Argives;
sentences.i: and was obeyed by as many people as you rule among the Argives;
sentences.n: πειθοίατο is the epic third plural optative of πείθομαι ‘obey’ (-οίατο for -οιντο), continuing the ‘whoever’ clause, and οἱ ‘to him’ is its dative. τοσσοίδ’ ὅσσοισιν is ‘as many as those over whom’, ἀνάσσεις ‘you rule’ taking the dative. Ἀργείοισιν ‘Argives’ has the epic dative plural -οισιν. The unit begins in mid-line and ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t: νῦν δέ σευ ὠνοσάμην πάγχυ φρένας, οἷον ἔειπες·
sentences.tr: nyn de seu ōnosamēn panchy phrenas, hoion eeipes·
sentences.l: But now of you I find fault with altogether the wits, such a thing you have said;
sentences.i: But now I find fault with your wits altogether, what a thing you have said;
sentences.n: σευ is the epic genitive of σύ, ‘of you’, and φρένας ‘wits’ is the part blamed: ‘I find fault with you in your wits’. ὠνοσάμην is the aorist of ὄνομαι ‘find fault with’, and the aorist expresses what is happening as he speaks. πάγχυ is ‘altogether’, and οἷον ἔειπες is an exclamatory relative, ‘what a thing you have said’.

sentences.t:
ὃς κέλεαι πολέμοιο συνεσταότος καὶ ἀϋτῆς
νῆας ἐϋσσέλμους ἅλαδ’ ἑλκέμεν, ὄφρ’ ἔτι μᾶλλον
Τρωσὶ μὲν εὐκτὰ γένηται ἐπικρατέουσί περ ἔμπης,
ἡμῖν δ’ αἰπὺς ὄλεθρος ἐπιρρέπῃ.
sentences.tr:
hos keleai polemoio synestaotos kai aÿtēs
nēas eÿsselmous halad’ helkemen, ophr’ eti mallon
Trōsi men eukta genētai epikrateousi per empēs,
hēmin d’ aipys olethros epirrepēi.
sentences.l:
you who bid, while war and battle-cry are joined,
the well-benched ships to drag seaward, so that still more
for the Trojans what is prayed for may come about, though they prevail all the same,
and for us steep destruction may incline.
sentences.i: you who bid us drag the well-benched ships to the sea while war and battle-cry are joined, so that what the Trojans pray for may come about still more, even though they prevail as it is, and steep destruction may tip toward us.
sentences.n: ὃς κέλεαι is ‘you who bid’, the relative picking up σέ; κέλεαι is the second singular of κέλομαι in its uncontracted form, and ἑλκέμεν the epic infinitive of ἕλκω. πολέμοιο συνεσταότος καὶ ἀϋτῆς is a genitive absolute, ‘war and battle-cry being joined’, with the perfect participle of συνίστημι. ὄφρ’ ἔτι μᾶλλον … γένηται is a purpose clause; εὐκτά is ‘what is prayed for’, a verbal adjective of εὔχομαι, and ἐπικρατέουσί περ ἔμπης is ‘even though they prevail all the same’. ἐπιρρέπῃ is a subjunctive of ἐπιρρέπω, the verb of a scale-pan dipping, with αἰπὺς ὄλεθρος ‘steep destruction’ as subject. The unit ends at the full stop in mid-line.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ Ἀχαιοὶ
σχήσουσιν πόλεμον νηῶν ἅλα δ’ ἑλκομενάων,
ἀλλ’ ἀποπαπτανέουσιν, ἐρωήσουσι δὲ χάρμης.
sentences.tr:
ou gar Achaioi
schēsousin polemon nēōn hala d’ helkomenaōn,
all’ apopaptaneousin, erōēsousi de charmēs.
sentences.l:
For the Achaeans will not
sustain the war when the ships are being dragged seaward,
but will look about in alarm, and will hold back from the joy of battle.
sentences.i: For the Achaeans will not sustain the war when the ships are dragged down to the sea, but will look about in alarm and hold back from the joy of battle.
sentences.n: σχήσουσιν is the future of ἔχω (stem σχ-); with πόλεμον it can mean ‘sustain the war’ or ‘hold off the war’, and the English takes the first because ἀλλά sets the opposite against it. νηῶν … ἑλκομενάων is a genitive absolute, ‘the ships being dragged’, with the epic feminine plural -άων. ἀποπαπτανέουσιν is built on παπταίνω ‘peer about’ and probably means ‘look about anxiously for a way out’; its exact sense is not certain. ἐρωήσουσι is the future of ἐρωέω ‘draw back’, with the genitive χάρμης ‘the joy of battle’. The unit begins in mid-line, after the full stop.

sentences.t: ἔνθά κε σὴ βουλὴ δηλήσεται ὄρχαμε λαῶν.
sentences.tr: entha ke sē boulē dēlēsetai orchame laōn.
sentences.l: Then your plan will do harm, chief of the people.”
sentences.i: In that case your plan will do harm, chief of the people.”
sentences.n: ἔνθά κε is ‘then, in that case’. δηλήσεται is the short-vowel subjunctive (or the future) of δηλέομαι ‘harm’, with σὴ βουλή ‘your plan’ as subject. ὄρχαμε λαῶν ‘chief of the people’ is a vocative of address, ὄρχαμος being a word of uncertain origin. The unit closes Odysseus’ speech.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγαμέμνων·
sentences.tr: ton d’ ēmeibet’ epeita anax andrōn Agamemnōn·
sentences.l: Him then answered the lord of men, Agamemnon:
sentences.i: Then Agamemnon, lord of men, answered him:
sentences.n: The same reply formula as 1.172: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα ‘and him then answered’, with ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν ‘lord of men’ as Agamemnon’s title. A new paragraph begins at 103.

sentences.t:
ὦ Ὀδυσεῦ μάλα πώς με καθίκεο θυμὸν ἐνιπῇ
ἀργαλέῃ·
sentences.tr:
ō Odyseu mala pōs me kathikeo thymon enipēi
argaleēi·
sentences.l:
“O Odysseus, very much, somehow, you have touched my heart with a rebuke
grievous;
sentences.i: “Odysseus, you have touched me deeply, to the heart, with a grievous rebuke;
sentences.n: ὦ Ὀδυσεῦ is the vocative of Ὀδυσσεύς, with a single σ. μάλα πώς, ‘very much, somehow’, is an intensifying idiom whose πώς is vague. καθίκεο is the epic aorist second singular of καθικνέομαι ‘reach, touch’, with με as object and θυμόν ‘heart’ as the part touched. ἐνιπῇ ἀργαλέῃ ‘with a grievous rebuke’ is a dative of means, with the epic ending -ῃ. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line.

sentences.t:
ἀτὰρ οὐ μὲν ἐγὼν ἀέκοντας ἄνωγα
νῆας ἐϋσσέλμους ἅλα δ’ ἑλκέμεν υἷας Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.tr:
atar ou men egōn aekontas anōga
nēas eÿsselmous hala d’ helkemen huias Achaiōn.
sentences.l:
but truly I do not bid unwilling ones
the well-benched ships to drag seaward, the sons of the Achaeans.
sentences.i: but I do not bid the sons of the Achaeans drag the well-benched ships to the sea against their will.
sentences.n: ἀτάρ ‘but’ is a by-form of αὐτάρ, and οὐ μέν ‘truly not’ is emphatic. ἀέκοντας ‘unwilling’ (ἀ- + ἑκών) is the object of ἄνωγα, a perfect with present sense, ‘I bid’, and agrees with υἷας Ἀχαιῶν ‘the sons of the Achaeans’, held to the end of the sentence. ἅλα δ’ is ἅλαδε ‘seaward’, written in two words as at 100. The unit begins in mid-line, after the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’ εἴη ὃς τῆσδέ γ’ ἀμείνονα μῆτιν ἐνίσποι
ἢ νέος ἠὲ παλαιός·
sentences.tr:
nyn d’ eiē hos tēsde g’ ameinona mētin enispoi
ē neos ēe palaios·
sentences.l:
But now may there be one who a better cunning than this may tell,
either young or old;
sentences.i: Now let there be someone, young or old, who can tell of a better cunning than this;
sentences.n: νῦν δ’ εἴη ὅς … ἐνίσποι is a wish put as a relative clause with the optative, ‘now may there be one who …’; ἐνίσποι is the aorist optative of ἐνέπω ‘tell’. τῆσδέ γ’ is the genitive of comparison after ἀμείνονα, ‘better than this’. μῆτις keeps its house rendering ‘cunning’ (the word means skill in devising, and ‘plan’ is kept for βουλή). ἢ νέος ἠὲ παλαιός is ‘either young or old’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line.

sentences.t: ἐμοὶ δέ κεν ἀσμένῳ εἴη.
sentences.tr: emoi de ken asmenōi eiē.
sentences.l: and to me, glad, it would be.”
sentences.i: and I should be glad of it.”
sentences.n: ἐμοὶ δέ κεν ἀσμένῳ εἴη is ‘and it would be to me, glad’: ἀσμένῳ is the dative of ἄσμενος ‘glad’, agreeing with ἐμοί, and the subject of εἴη is the better plan. The unit begins in mid-line, after the ano teleia, and closes Agamemnon’s speech.
